Anatomy Reference

Hand & Fingers

Flexors · Extensors · Intrinsic Muscles · Pulleys · Growth Plates

Flexor Tendons & Muscles

The flexor system of the hand runs through the carpal tunnel and fibro-osseous tunnels (sheaths) of each finger, divided into extrinsic muscles (belly in the forearm) and the intrinsic lumbricals. Click any image for full detail.

Extrinsic Flexors — Forearm Origin

Image Muscle Origin Insertion Action
Flexor Digitorum Profundus (FDP) Proximal ¾ of anterior ulna; interosseous membrane Distal phalanx bases of digits 2–5 (volar) Flexes DIP, PIP, MCP; wrist flexion (weak)
Flexor Digitorum Superficialis (FDS) Medial epicondyle (common flexor tendon); coronoid process; radius (oblique line) Middle phalanx bases of digits 2–5 (splits around FDP) Flexes PIP & MCP; wrist flexion
Flexor Pollicis Longus (FPL) Anterior radius; interosseous membrane; medial epicondyle (variable) Distal phalanx of thumb (volar base) Flexes IP of thumb; assists MCP & CMC flexion
Flexor Carpi Radialis (FCR) Medial epicondyle (common flexor tendon) Base of 2nd metacarpal (±3rd) Wrist flexion; radial deviation
Flexor Carpi Ulnaris (FCU) Medial epicondyle; medial olecranon & posterior ulna Pisiform → hamate → 5th metacarpal base Wrist flexion; ulnar deviation
Palmaris Longus Absent ~14% Medial epicondyle (common flexor tendon) Palmar aponeurosis; flexor retinaculum Tenses palmar aponeurosis; weak wrist flexor
Camper's Chiasm: The FDS tendon splits at the level of the proximal phalanx to allow the FDP tendon to pass through — called Camper's chiasm (chiasma tendinum). The FDS reunites briefly before inserting on the middle phalanx.
Zones of Injury (Verdan): Zone II ("no-man's land") from the A1 pulley to the FDS insertion is the most surgically challenging zone due to the two tendons sharing the fibrous sheath.

Extensor Tendons & Muscles

Extensor tendons run in six synovial compartments at the wrist, held by the extensor retinaculum. Distally they form the complex extensor mechanism (dorsal apparatus) via contributions from intrinsic muscles.

Extrinsic Extensors — Forearm Origin

Image Muscle Compartment Origin Insertion Action
Abductor Pollicis Longus (APL) & Extensor Pollicis Brevis (EPB) 1 APL: posterior ulna & radius; EPB: posterior radius APL → 1st MC base; EPB → proximal phalanx thumb Thumb abduction & extension; radial deviation
Extensor Carpi Radialis Longus (ECRL) & Brevis (ECRB) 2 ECRL: lateral supracondylar ridge; ECRB: lateral epicondyle ECRL → 2nd MC base; ECRB → 3rd MC base Wrist extension; radial deviation
Extensor Digitorum Communis (EDC) 4 Lateral epicondyle (common extensor tendon) Extensor expansion (dorsal hood) of digits 2–5 Extends MCP (primarily); assists PIP/DIP extension
Extensor Indicis Proprius (EIP) 4 Posterior ulna (distal); interosseous membrane Extensor expansion of index finger (ulnar to EDC) Independent index finger extension
Extensor Digiti Minimi (EDM) 5 Lateral epicondyle (common extensor tendon) Extensor expansion of little finger Independent little finger extension
Extensor Carpi Ulnaris (ECU) 6 Lateral epicondyle; posterior ulnar border 5th metacarpal base (ulnar side) Wrist extension; ulnar deviation
Extensor Pollicis Longus (EPL) 3 Posterior ulna (middle third); interosseous membrane Distal phalanx of thumb (dorsal base) Extends IP & MCP of thumb; retropulsion; radial deviation
Anatomical Snuffbox: Bounded radially by APL & EPB (compartment 1), ulnarly by EPL (compartment 3). The scaphoid and radial artery lie at its floor — tenderness here after a fall suggests scaphoid fracture.
Extensor Mechanism (Dorsal Apparatus): The EDC tendon broadens at the MCP joint into the sagittal bands, then the central slip (inserts P2) and two lateral bands (from intrinsics + EDC) which converge into the terminal tendon inserting on P3.

Wrist Extensor Compartments

CompartmentContentsClinical Note
1APL, EPBDe Quervain tenosynovitis
2ECRL, ECRBIntersection syndrome (at crossing with C1)
3EPLRupture after distal radius fractures (Lister's tubercle)
4EDC, EIPMost tendons; widest compartment
5EDMDRUJ capsule is roof
6ECUECU tendinopathy; instability with TFCC tears

Muscles of the Hand

Intrinsic muscles originate and insert within the hand. They form three groups: thenar (thumb), hypothenar (little finger), and the central compartment (lumbricals and interossei).

Thenar Muscles

Image Muscle Origin Insertion Action
Abductor Pollicis Brevis (APB) Scaphoid tubercle; trapezium ridge; flexor retinaculum Radial base of proximal phalanx of thumb Palmar abduction of thumb (perpendicular to palm)
Flexor Pollicis Brevis (FPB) Superficial head: flexor retinaculum & trapezium; Deep head: trapezoid & capitate Radial base of proximal phalanx of thumb; radial sesamoid Flexes MCP joint of thumb; assists opposition
Opponens Pollicis (OP) Trapezium tubercle; flexor retinaculum Radial shaft of 1st metacarpal (entire length) Flexes, medially rotates, and adducts 1st metacarpal — brings thumb pad to face other digits (opposition)
Adductor Pollicis (AdP) Oblique head: capitate & bases of MC2–3; Transverse head: anterior shaft of MC3 Ulnar base of proximal phalanx of thumb; ulnar sesamoid Adducts thumb toward palm; assists MCP flexion of thumb

Hypothenar Muscles

Image Muscle Origin Insertion Action
Abductor Digiti Minimi (ADM) Pisiform; pisohamate ligament; tendon of FCU Ulnar base of proximal phalanx of little finger; ulnar extensor expansion Abducts little finger; flexes MCP of little finger
Flexor Digiti Minimi Brevis (FDMB) Hook of hamate; flexor retinaculum Ulnar base of proximal phalanx of little finger Flexes MCP joint of little finger
Opponens Digiti Minimi (ODM) Hook of hamate; flexor retinaculum Ulnar border of 5th metacarpal shaft (entire length) Flexes and laterally rotates 5th metacarpal; deepens the palm (cups the hand)

Lumbricals & Interossei

Image Muscle Origin Insertion Action
Lumbricals (1–4) Radial side(s) of FDP tendons to digits 2–5 Radial side of extensor expansion of digits 2–5 Flexes MCP joints; extends PIP and DIP joints simultaneously
Dorsal Interossei (DI 1–4) DAB Adjacent sides of all metacarpals (bipennate — each from two MCs) Bases of proximal phalanges and extensor expansions of digits 2–4 Abducts fingers away from midline (D3); flexes MCP joints; extends PIP and DIP joints
Palmar Interossei (PI 1–3) PAD Metacarpal shafts (unipennate — ulnar side of MC2; radial side of MC4 & MC5) Bases of proximal phalanges and extensor expansions of digits 2, 4 & 5 Adducts fingers toward midline (D3); flexes MCP joints; extends PIP and DIP joints
Memory Aid: DAB — Dorsal interossei Abduct. PAD — Palmar interossei Adduct. The reference axis is the middle finger (D3).

Flexor Tendon Pulleys

Annular (A) and cruciate (C) pulleys form the fibro-osseous sheath that holds flexor tendons close to bone, converting muscle contraction into efficient digital flexion. The A2 and A4 pulleys are the most biomechanically critical.

Finger Pulley System (Digits 2–5)

Pulley Type Location Origin Clinical Significance
A1 Annular MCP joint (volar plate) Volar plate of MCP Trigger finger — stenosing tenosynovitis at A1
A2 ★ Annular — Critical Proximal half of P1 Periosteum of P1 Most important; must preserve in surgery; rock-climbing "pulley tear"
C1 Cruciate Distal P1 Retinacular ligaments Less critical; allows sheath flexibility
A3 Annular PIP joint (volar plate) Volar plate of PIP May be released without significant bowstringing
C2 Cruciate Proximal P2 Retinacular ligaments Allows flexion without bulge
A4 ★ Annular — Critical Middle third of P2 Periosteum of P2 Second most important; DIP flexion efficiency
C3 Cruciate Distal P2 Retinacular ligaments Thin; often absent
A5 Annular DIP joint (volar plate) Volar plate of DIP Small; often preserved in flexor repair

Thumb Pulley System

Pulley Location Origin Note
A1MCP jointVolar plate of MCPTrigger thumb release site
Oblique ★P1 shaftPeriosteum of P1Most critical thumb pulley (analogous to A2)
A2IP jointVolar plate of IPSmall; variable
Rock Climbing Pulley Injuries: The A2 pulley of the ring finger is the most commonly ruptured in climbers (crimping position). A partial tear (grade I–II) is managed conservatively; full rupture (grade III–IV) may require surgical repair or H-pulley reconstruction.
Trigger Finger (Stenosing Tenosynovitis): Thickening of the A1 pulley causes catching or locking of the flexor tendon. Treatment: corticosteroid injection into the sheath or A1 pulley release.

Growth Plates of the Hand & Fingers

Physes (growth plates) in the hand follow a unique pattern: metacarpals have a physis at the base (except MC1 which is at the head), while phalanges have their physis at the base. This has important implications for fracture patterns in skeletally immature patients.

Physeal Locations — Summary

Bone Physis Location Appears (X-ray) Closes Clinical Note
MC1 (Thumb) ★ Unique HEAD (distal) ~2 yrs (F), ~3 yrs (M) 14–16 yrs (F), 16–18 yrs (M) Only MC with distal physis; Salter-Harris fractures near MCP
MC2–5 BASE (proximal) ~2–3 yrs 14–16 yrs (F), 16–18 yrs (M) Boxer's fracture involves metaphysis/neck, not physis
Proximal Phalanx (P1) BASE (proximal) ~2 yrs 14–16 yrs (F), 16–18 yrs (M) Most common finger fracture in children (SH II); Seymour fracture at distal P1
Middle Phalanx (P2) BASE (proximal) ~2–3 yrs 14–16 yrs (F), 15–18 yrs (M) Volar plate avulsion vs physis injury distinction important
Distal Phalanx (P3) BASE (proximal) ~1–2 yrs 13–15 yrs (F), 15–17 yrs (M) Seymour fracture: open SH I/II at P3 base — nail fold displaced over physis

Key Fracture Patterns in the Immature Hand

Fracture / Eponym Location Mechanism Management Pearl
Seymour Fracture Distal P3 physis (SH I or II) Axial load + flexion at DIP Open fracture (nail fold displaced); requires I&D, nail removal, K-wire; do not miss
Extra-octave Fracture MC5 neck/base Greater remodeling potential in children; acceptable angulation higher than adults
Gamekeeper's / Skier's Thumb P1 base of thumb (UCL avulsion) Forced radial deviation MCP In children, physis fractures (SH III) instead of ligament tear; check X-ray before stress test
Mallet Finger (bony) P3 base dorsal fragment (SH III) Forced DIP flexion (extensor avulsion) Immobilize DIP in extension 6–8 wks; surgery if >30% articular surface or volar subluxation
Pseudo-boutonnière (SH III PIP) P2 base volar Dorsal dislocation / hyperextension May mimic volar plate injury; look for physeal line on lateral X-ray
Seymour Fracture Pearl: This is an open fracture even if it appears benign on X-ray — the germinal nail matrix is interposed in the fracture site. Untreated it leads to osteomyelitis, nail deformity, and physeal arrest. Must be treated surgically as an emergency.
MC1 vs MC2–5 Memory Aid: "The thumb does the opposite" — its physis is at the HEAD, while all other metacarpals have their physis at the BASE. This mirrors the phalanges (all base) but is unique among metacarpals.
Salter-Harris Classification: Type I (physis only) → Type V (crush). Types II & III are most common in the hand. Type III (intra-articular) requires anatomic reduction. Always compare with contralateral films in ambiguous cases.
